p.t: A Bad Day in Chiang Mai
p.x:
Last year, my friend and I went to Chiang Mai, but our first day was terrible. First, we got lost in the old town because my phone was broken and we didn't have a map. Then it started to rain, and I had forgotten my umbrella at the hotel!
We wanted to visit a famous temple, but when we arrived, it was closed. We had to wait for a taxi for forty minutes. While we were waiting, a mosquito bit me, and soon I had ten bites on my arms!
In the evening, I called my mum. "Don't worry," she said. "Tomorrow will be better." She was right. The next day, the sun was shining, and we had a wonderful time.

Travelling is exciting, but problems can happen. Here is some advice for the most common ones.
Lost bags: If your suitcase doesn't arrive at baggage reclaim, go to the airline desk immediately. Keep your boarding pass and luggage tag. You may be able to claim money to buy clothes.
Theft: In busy tourist areas, pickpockets are common. If your wallet or passport is stolen, report the theft to the police. If you lose your passport, contact your country's embassy.
Car problems: If you have a breakdown or a flat tyre, call the rental company. They will send a mechanic. If a road is closed, follow the detour signs.
Health: Avoid sunburn by using sun cream, and be careful with street food: food poisoning can ruin a holiday. If you feel homesick, call your family; it usually helps.
Other problems: Check whether you need a visa before you go, and find out what you can bring through customs and across the border. If there's a strike, your flight may be rescheduled. Finally, if there's a mix-up with your hotel booking, stay calm. A phrasebook can help you explain. Don't forget to ask at lost property if you leave something on a train.

No matter how carefully we plan, travel rarely goes exactly as expected. Flights are cancelled, connecting flights are missed and unforeseen events, from volcanic eruptions to strikes, can leave thousands of passengers stranded. How travellers respond to such problems often says more about them than the trip itself.
Experienced travellers tend to see setbacks as part of the adventure. They know that a misunderstanding with a taxi driver who seems to overcharge may simply be a language problem, and that a calm, polite approach usually achieves more than anger. When things do go seriously wrong, they also know their rights. In many regions, airlines must pay compensation for long delays, and hotels may offer a discount for the inconvenience if a room is not as advertised.
Some challenges are physical. Visitors to high places such as the Andes or Tibet may suffer from altitude sickness, with headaches and breathlessness, and must ascend slowly. Others are psychological. Culture shock, the confusion and anxiety that can follow arrival in an unfamiliar country, is surprisingly common, even among confident travellers. Typically, it passes through stages, from initial excitement to frustration and, eventually, acceptance.
Perhaps the most valuable lesson is that problems can become the most memorable parts of a journey. Years later, few people remember the perfect day at the beach; they remember the predicament they found themselves in and how they managed to cope.
